A **molecular** absorber gives **bands**, and absorbing from white light gives an
**absorption** spectrum.
**Step 1 — decide emission or absorption.** White light - a **continuous** spectrum -
passes **through** the solution, which removes certain wavelengths ✓ What emerges is
therefore an **absorption** spectrum, with dark regions on a bright background.
**Step 2 — decide lines or bands.** Potassium permanganate in solution absorbs as
**molecules**, not as free atoms ✓ A molecule has closely spaced **vibrational** and
**rotational** levels superimposed on each electronic level, so its transitions crowd
together into broad **bands** rather than sharp lines.
**Step 3 — conclude.** A **band absorption spectrum** ✓
**Why the solution looks purple.** It absorbs strongly in the **green-yellow**, around
525 nm ✓ and transmits the red and blue ends, whose combination the eye perceives as
the characteristic deep purple of permanganate.
**When line spectra appear instead.** From **free atoms** - a sodium flame, a hydrogen
discharge, the Sun's atmosphere ✓ There the energy levels are sharp and well separated,
so the absorption or emission is confined to narrow lines.
**The four kinds of spectrum, distinguished.**
**continuous**: hot dense source - a filament, the photosphere ✓
**line emission**: hot rarefied **atoms** - a discharge tube
**line absorption**: cool **atoms** before a continuous source - Fraunhofer lines ✓
**band**: **molecules**, in emission or absorption ✓ as here
**Why molecular levels are so closely spaced.** Electronic transitions are of order
**eV**; vibrational **0·1 eV**; rotational **0·001 eV** ✓ Each electronic transition is
therefore accompanied by a whole ladder of vibrational and rotational possibilities,
blurring into a band.
**Where band spectra are used.** To identify **molecules** in cool stars, comets,
planetary atmospheres and interstellar clouds ✓ and in the laboratory as the basis of
infrared spectroscopy, which identifies chemical bonds by their vibrational bands.
**Why "dilute" is specified.** A concentrated solution would absorb nearly everything
and the spectrum would be too dark to read ✓ Dilution leaves the characteristic bands
visible against transmitted light.
**Reading the distractors.** **Line absorption** ✗ would need free atoms. The two
**emission** options ✗ would need the solution to be a source of light, not an
absorber ✓
∴ band absorption spectrum.

Light from the man bends **towards the normal** on entering the water, so he appears
**taller** than he is.
**Step 1 — follow a ray from the man's head.** It travels through air and strikes the
water surface **obliquely** ✓ Entering the denser medium, it bends **towards** the
normal.
**Step 2 — see where the fish traces it back to.** The fish, looking along the
refracted ray, projects it back in a straight line ✓ That backward projection meets the
vertical through the man **higher** than his actual head.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The man's head appears **raised**, so he looks **taller** than
he really is ✓
**Why his feet are not raised as much.** Rays from his feet, near the water's edge,
strike the surface at a different angle ✓ The apparent displacement grows with the
angle from the normal, so the top of him is lifted more than the bottom - and he is
**stretched** vertically.
**The companion effect.** To the **man** looking down, the **fish** appears **raised**
and so **nearer the surface** than it is ✓ which is why a spear fisherman must aim
**below** the apparent position of the fish.
**The reciprocity.** Both effects follow from the same Snell's law, applied in opposite
directions ✓ The man is lifted for the fish; the fish is lifted for the man. Each sees
the other displaced **upward**.
**Snell's window.** The fish's entire view of the world above is compressed into a
**cone of half-angle 48·8°** ✓ the critical angle for water. Outside that circular
window it sees only the reflected pond bottom - a striking sight in underwater
photographs.
**Why the apparent height increases without limit near the edge.** As the angle of
incidence approaches **90°**, the refracted ray approaches the critical angle and the
apparent elevation grows sharply ✓ Objects at the very rim of Snell's window appear
enormously stretched.
**The near-normal case, for contrast.** Looking straight up, the fish sees objects at
their proper **angular** size but displaced in depth by the factor n ✓ The distortion
is purely a consequence of the **oblique** view, which is why the question specifies
it.
**Reading the distractors.** **Shorter** ✗ reverses the refraction. **Same height** ✗
would need no refraction at all - true only for a ray along the normal. **Depends on
the obliquity** ✗ - the **amount** does, but the man always looks **taller**, never
shorter ✓
∴ taller than what he actually is.

By Torricelli's law the emptying time goes as **√h**, so half the depth takes
**1/√2** of the time.
**Step 1 — recall the efflux speed.**
v = **√(2gh)** ✓ Torricelli's theorem, which is Bernoulli's equation applied to a hole.
**Step 2 — write the emptying time.** For a vessel of uniform cross-section A draining
through an orifice of area a:
t = (A/a)√(2h/g) ✓
so **t ∝ √h**.
**Step 3 — compare the two cases.**
t_half/t_full = √(h/2)/√h
= **1/√2 = 0·707** ✓
**Step 4 — compute.**
t_half = 10 x 0·707
= 7·07
≈ **7 minutes** ✓
**Why it is not 5 minutes.** The flow is **not** steady ✓ As the level falls the
pressure head falls with it, so the outflow slows continuously. Half the water drains
in **more** than half the time - 7 minutes rather than 5.
**A check from the other end.** Draining the **upper** half of a full vessel takes
10 − 7·07 = **2·93 minutes**, while the **lower** half takes 7·07 ✓ The first half
empties fast, under a high head; the last half dawdles.
**Where the √h comes from.** Integrating A dh/dt = −a√(2gh) ✓
t = (A/a)√(2/g) x √h, so the time to empty from depth h is proportional to √h.
**Why the orifice area matters only as a ratio.** t depends on **A/a** ✓ A wide vessel
with a small hole takes a long time; the shape of the vessel enters only through its
cross-section.
**The assumptions behind Torricelli's law.** The vessel is **wide** compared with the
orifice, so the surface falls slowly; the liquid is ideal; and the flow is streamline ✓
Real orifices have a contraction coefficient of about 0·62, which lengthens the time but
does not change the √h dependence.
**A worked instance.** A tank 1 m deep draining through a hole with A/a = 100:
t = 100√(2/9·8) = **45·2 s** when full ✓ and 32 s from half full.
**Reading the distractors.** **5 minutes** ✗ assumes a constant flow rate - the
commonest error. **9 minutes** ✗ and **3 minutes** ✗ correspond to depth ratios of 0·81
and 0·09 ✓ Only 1/√2 follows from Torricelli's law.
∴ 7 minutes.

At 50° from glass to air the ray is **beyond the critical angle**, so it is **totally
internally reflected** - and the deviation is 80°.
**Step 1 — find the critical angle.**
sin C = 1/n = 1/1·5 = 0·667
**C = 41·8°** ✓
**Step 2 — compare with the angle of incidence.**
50° **>** 41·8° ✓ so the ray does **not** emerge. It undergoes **total internal
reflection**.
**Step 3 — find the deviation for a reflection.** A reflected ray turns through
δ = 180° − 2i
= 180° − 100°
= **80°** ✓
**Why the refraction formula does not apply.** Snell's law would give
sin r = 1·5 sin 50° = **1·149** ✗ greater than 1, which has no solution ✓ That
impossibility **is** total internal reflection, and it is the signal that the first two
options - both built on a refracted ray - are empty.
**The two conditions for total internal reflection.**
light must travel from **denser to rarer** ✓ here glass to air
the angle of incidence must **exceed** the critical angle ✓ 50° > 41·8°
Both are satisfied.
**Why the reflection is total.** **100%** of the light is returned, with no transmitted
beam at all ✓ Unlike a silvered mirror, which absorbs a few per cent, this reflection
is perfect - which is why prisms are preferred to mirrors in binoculars and
periscopes.
**The deviation formula, derived.** The reflected ray makes angle i with the normal on
the other side, so the angle between the incident and reflected directions is
180° − 2i ✓ At normal incidence the deviation is 180° - straight back; at grazing
incidence it approaches zero.
**A check at the critical angle itself.** At exactly 41·8° the refracted ray **grazes**
the surface ✓ and the reflection becomes total only beyond it.
**Why the question is a good one.** It looks like a routine refraction problem ✓ The
whole difficulty is recognising that no refraction occurs - which requires computing
the critical angle first, before reaching for Snell's law.
**Where this is exploited.** **Optical fibres**, where light is trapped by repeated
total reflection; **diamond's** brilliance, with a critical angle of only 24°; and the
**mirage**, where gradual refraction in hot air produces the same effect ✓
**Reading the distractors.** The two options with **sin⁻¹(sin 50°/1·5)** ✗ assume a
refracted ray that does not exist. **0°** ✗ would mean the ray passed straight on ✓
∴ 80°.

Use **λ = h/√(2mqV)** for a charged particle accelerated through a potential
difference.
**Step 1 — write the momentum.** The proton gains kinetic energy qV:
½mv² = qV
p = **√(2mqV)** ✓
**Step 2 — apply de Broglie's relation.**
λ = h/p = **h/√(2mqV)** ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate the denominator.**
2mqV = 2(1·6 x 10⁻²⁷)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)(10³)
= **5·12 x 10⁻⁴³** ✓
√(5·12 x 10⁻⁴³) = **7·16 x 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹**
**Step 4 — divide.**
λ = 6·63 x 10⁻³⁴/(7·16 x 10⁻²²)
= **9·3 x 10⁻¹³ ≈ 0·9 x 10⁻¹² m** ✓
**In other units.** 0·9 x 10⁻¹² m = **0·9 pm = 0·009 Å** ✓ far smaller than an atom -
about a hundredth of an ångström.
**Why so much shorter than an electron's.** At the same voltage the proton is **1836
times** heavier, so its momentum is √1836 = **43 times** greater ✓ and its wavelength
43 times shorter. An electron at 1 kV has λ = 0·39 Å; the proton has 0·009 Å.
**The useful shortcut for protons.**
λ = **0·0286/√V nm** ✓
Here √1000 = 31·6, giving 0·0286/31·6 = **9·05 x 10⁻⁴ nm = 0·9 pm** ✓ confirming the
answer in one step.
**Why such a short wavelength matters.** Resolution is limited by wavelength ✓ Proton
and ion beams can in principle resolve finer detail than electrons at the same energy -
which is the principle of the **helium-ion microscope**.
**A check on the energy.** 1 keV for a proton is a modest energy ✓ Its speed is
v = √(2qV/m) = **4·4 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹**, only 0·15% of c, so relativistic corrections are
negligible.
**The dimensional check.**
[h/√(mqV)] = (J s)/√(kg x C x V) = (J s)/√(kg J) = (J s)/√(kg J) ✓ which reduces to
metres.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·9 nm** ✗ is a thousand times too large. **7 Å** ✗ and
**600 Å** ✗ are larger still ✓ A proton at 1 keV must have a wavelength far **below**
an ångström, which settles it at a glance.
∴ 0.9 × 10⁻¹² m.

Equal heat flow through two identical rods in series gives a **conductivity-weighted
average** of the end temperatures.
**Step 1 — write the heat flow through each rod.** The rods are identical in length and
area, so with the junction at T:
through AC: k₁A(100 − T)/L
through CB: k₂A(T − 25)/L ✓
**Step 2 — equate them.** In the steady state no heat accumulates at C:
k₁(100 − T) = k₂(T − 25) ✓
**Step 3 — substitute k₁ : k₂ = 2 : 3.**
2(100 − T) = 3(T − 25)
200 − 2T = 3T − 75 ✓
**Step 4 — solve.**
275 = 5T
**T = 55 °C** ✓
**The weighted-average form.**
T = (k₁T₁ + k₂T₂)/(k₁ + k₂) ✓
= [2(100) + 3(25)]/5
= 275/5
= **55 °C** ✓ in one line.
**Why the junction lies nearer the cold end.** The **better** conductor - here CB, with
k₂ = 3 - needs a **smaller** temperature drop to carry the same heat ✓ So most of the
75 °C difference falls across the poorer conductor AC.
**The two drops.**
across AC: 100 − 55 = **45 °C**
across CB: 55 − 25 = **30 °C** ✓
and 45 : 30 = 3 : 2, the **inverse** of the conductivity ratio - exactly as the equal
heat flow demands.
**The thermal-resistance view.** R_th ∝ 1/k, so the resistances are in the ratio
**3 : 2** ✓ and the 75 °C divides in that proportion: 45 and 30. It is a potential
divider in thermal disguise.
**A check on the heat flow.** Taking kA/L = 1 for k = 1:
through AC: 2 x 45 = **90**
through CB: 3 x 30 = **90** ✓ equal, as required.
**Why the rods must be identical in dimensions.** Only then does the area and length
cancel, leaving the conductivities alone ✓ Different dimensions would call for the full
kA/L in each term.
**What "steady state" means.** The temperatures have stopped changing ✓ Before that the
specific heats matter and the problem becomes a differential equation.
**Reading the distractors.** **50 °C** ✗ is the plain average, right only for equal
conductivities. **75 °C** ✗ and **60 °C** ✗ place the junction too close to the hot
end ✓ The better conductor is on the **cold** side, so the junction must lie below the
midpoint of 62·5 °C.
∴ 55°C.

"Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular" is **Brewster's condition**, from which the
critical angle follows.
**Step 1 — apply Brewster's law.** When the reflected and refracted rays are at 90°,
i + r = 90° and
**n = tan i** ✓
**Step 2 — write the critical angle.** For the same pair of media,
sin C = 1/n ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
sin C = 1/tan i = **cot i**
**C = sin⁻¹(cot i)** ✓
**Why the two angles are related at all.** Both are determined by the single number n ✓
Brewster's angle fixes n as tan i; the critical angle then follows from sin C = 1/n
without any further information.
**A worked instance.** For glass with n = 1·5:
Brewster's angle: i = tan⁻¹(1·5) = **56·3°** ✓
cot i = 1/1·5 = **0·667**
C = sin⁻¹(0·667) = **41·8°** ✓ exactly the critical angle for glass, confirming the
formula.
**The constraint this implies.** For C to exist we need cot i ≤ 1, that is **i ≥ 45°** ✓
And indeed Brewster's angle exceeds 45° whenever n > 1 - which is always, for light
entering a denser medium.
**What is special about Brewster's angle.** The reflected light is **completely
plane-polarised**, with its electric field perpendicular to the plane of incidence ✓
The refracted ray sets the medium's electrons oscillating along the direction the
reflected ray would take, and a dipole cannot radiate along its own axis.
**The everyday consequence.** Glare from water, glass and wet roads is reflected near
Brewster's angle and is strongly polarised ✓ Polarising sunglasses are cut to block the
horizontal component and so remove most of it.
**The direction of travel differs between the two.** Brewster's angle applies going
from **rarer to denser**; the critical angle only going from **denser to rarer** ✓ The
question links the two by way of the shared refractive index.
**Reading the distractors.** **sin⁻¹(tan i)** ✗ gives a value greater than 1 for
i > 45°, which has no inverse sine. **tan⁻¹(sin i)** ✗ and **cos⁻¹(tan i)** ✗ follow
from no relation between the two angles ✓ Testing with n = 1·5 and i = 56·3° eliminates
all three at once.
∴ Sin⁻¹(Cot i).
